summary.text: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that describes how likely an event is, often written as a percentage from 0% to 100%.
For a fair coin, heads and tails are equally probable, so each has a probability of 1/2, also written 0.5 or 50%.
People read probability in two main ways: as the relative frequency of an outcome in the long run, or as a degree of belief.

facts.label: Fair coin
facts.value: Heads and tails each get probability 1/2

facts.label: Cardano’s odds
facts.value: Defined odds as favourable outcomes against unfavourable ones

facts.label: Earliest treatment
facts.value: Huygens gave the earliest known scientific treatment in 1657

items.prompt: A factory tests one machine part many thousands of times and reports how often it fails. Which reading of probability is this?

options.label: Degree of belief, held before any testing
Relative frequency across repeated trials
A tendency in one single trial
Expert knowledge turned into a prior

items.explain: Frequentist probability is the relative frequency of an outcome when an experiment is repeated indefinitely.

items.prompt: An analyst starts with an expert’s prior view, then folds in new experimental data to reach a final probability. Which approach is this?

options.label: Frequentist probability
Propensity probability
The theory of errors
Bayesian probability

items.explain: Bayesian probability combines expert knowledge, as a prior, with experimental data to produce probabilities.

items.prompt: A raffle drum holds some prize tickets and some blanks. Which ratio gives the probability of drawing a prize?

options.label: Prizes out of all tickets in the drum
Prizes compared with blanks
Blanks out of all tickets in the drum
Blanks compared with prizes

items.explain: Odds compare favourable to unfavourable outcomes, which implies probability is favourable outcomes over all possible outcomes.

items.prompt: A fair coin lands heads or tails and nothing else. What fixes the chance of heads at 1/2?

options.label: Each flip cancels out the one before it
The coin must alternate between its two sides
Tails is always twice as likely
The two outcomes are equally probable and nothing else can happen

items.explain: Both outcomes are equally probable and no other outcome is possible, so each gets 1/2.

items.prompt: A forecaster says an event has probability 1.4. Why can that not be right?

options.label: Probabilities must be whole numbers
A probability is a number between 0 and 1
Only coins can have probabilities
Percentages cannot be turned into decimals

items.explain: A probability lies between 0 and 1, or 0% and 100% as a percentage.

items.prompt: Before the middle of the seventeenth century, what did calling an opinion “probable” mean?

options.label: That it was approvable, the kind sensible people would hold
That it had been measured by repeated experiments
That it was more likely than not to be true
That a witness had sworn to it in court

items.explain: Back then “probable” meant approvable, applied to opinion and action, unlike the modern weight of empirical evidence.
